title: NumPy arrays, shapes and broadcasting
description: Strides, views versus copies, dimension prepending, trailing axis expansion, axis reductions, and vectorization rules in NumPy.

questions.text: Given array a of shape (3, 1) and array b of shape (4,), what is the shape of a + b under NumPy broadcasting rules?

options.text: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3, 1) and (4,)
(3, 4), because NumPy prepends 1 to b making it (1, 4), then stretches both arrays along singleton axes
(4, 3), because 1D arrays take precedence on the leading axis
(3, 1), because b is truncated to match the column count of a

questions.explanation: NumPy broadcasting compares trailing dimensions right to left. b has shape (4,), so NumPy prepends 1 to align ranks: (1, 4). Then dimension 1 of a (size 1) stretches to 4, and dimension 0 of b (size 1) stretches to 3, producing a broadcasted shape of (3, 4).

questions.text: You execute sub = arr[0:2, 0:2] on a 2D NumPy array arr, and then set sub[0, 0] = 999. What happens to arr[0, 0]?

options.text: arr[0, 0] is unchanged because basic slicing always returns an independent memory copy
arr[0, 0] is updated to 999 because basic slice indexing returns a view sharing the same data buffer
NumPy throws a ReadOnlyBufferError unless arr.copy() was explicitly called
arr[0, 0] updates only if arr is C-contiguous, but remains unchanged if Fortran-ordered

questions.explanation: Basic slicing with slice objects (start:stop:step) returns a view pointing to the same underlying data buffer with modified shape and strides. Mutating a view modifies the base array. In contrast, advanced indexing (with boolean masks or integer arrays) creates an independent copy.

questions.text: For a 2D array X of shape (100, 10), what does X.sum(axis=0) return?

options.text: A 1D array of shape (10,) containing the column sums
A 1D array of shape (100,) containing the row sums
A scalar containing the sum of all 1,000 elements
A 2D array of shape (100, 1) with preserved row dimensions

questions.explanation: Specifying axis=0 collapses dimension 0 (the 100 rows), aggregating across rows to produce the sum for each of the 10 columns. To sum each row across columns, use axis=1.

questions.text: Boolean mask indexing arr[arr > 0] returns a memory view of arr, so mutating it modifies arr in place.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Boolean indexing is advanced indexing. Because the matching elements may not follow a regular strided stepping in memory, NumPy must allocate a fresh 1D array and copy the matching elements into it. Mutating the resulting array does not modify arr.

questions.text: Why is np.linalg.solve(A, b) preferred over np.linalg.inv(A) @ b for solving linear systems Ax = b in numerical ML?

options.text: np.linalg.solve uses LU/Cholesky decomposition directly without forming the inverse, making it both faster and significantly more numerically stable
np.linalg.inv works only for diagonal matrices, while solve works on all matrices
np.linalg.solve automatically performs L2 regularization if the matrix is singular
There is no difference in accuracy; solve is simply syntactic sugar for inv(A) @ b

questions.explanation: Explicitly computing the matrix inverse A^(-1) squares the condition number error and requires ~2x more floating point operations. solve(A, b) performs triangular factorizations (LU or Cholesky) and backward substitution, preserving numerical precision and avoiding catastrophic cancellation on near-singular matrices.

questions.text: What does a[:, np.newaxis] do to a 1D NumPy array a of shape (N,)?

options.text: Flattens the array into a scalar
Converts it into a 2D column vector of shape (N, 1)
Converts it into a 2D row vector of shape (1, N)
Copies the array N times along a new memory axis

questions.explanation: np.newaxis (an alias for None) inserts a new axis of length 1 at that position. Placing it in the column slot transforms shape (N,) into a 2D column vector of shape (N, 1) without copying underlying memory.
